common_triggers: used a variable before assigning it
explanation: Python raised this because it tried to look up a variable name that doesn't exist yet in any accessible scope.
likely_causes: The variable was never defined before this line ran
The variable name is misspelled somewhere
The variable was defined inside a function or block and isn't visible outside it
The variable was defined after the line that uses it
debugging_steps: Read the exact variable name in the error message
Search the file for where that name is first assigned
Check for spelling or case differences (Python is case-sensitive)
Check whether the assignment happens inside a function, loop, or conditional that may not have run
Confirm the assignment happens before the line that uses the variable
fix_pattern: Define the variable before it is used, correct the spelling, or move the assignment to a scope visible at the point of use.
learning_concept: Python variable scope and the order of execution
practice_seed: Give the user a snippet where a variable is defined inside an if-block that doesn't execute, and ask them to fix it so the variable is always defined.

common_triggers: argument must be str, not int
explanation: Python raised this because an operation or function was used with a value of a type it doesn't support.
likely_causes: Mixing incompatible types in an operation, e.g. string + integer
Calling a variable that isn't actually a function
Passing the wrong type of argument to a built-in or library function
Forgetting to convert user input (which is always a string) before using it numerically
debugging_steps: Read which operation or function call triggered the error
Print or check the type() of each value involved
Check whether input from a file, API, or user needs explicit conversion
Check the documentation for the expected argument types
fix_pattern: Convert the value to the expected type before the operation, or adjust the function call to match expected argument types.
learning_concept: Python data types and type conversion
practice_seed: Give the user a snippet that adds a string and an integer, and ask them to fix the type mismatch.

explanation: Python raised this because the code tried to access a position in a list (or other sequence) that doesn't exist.
likely_causes: Using an index equal to or greater than the length of the list
Off-by-one error in a loop range
Assuming a list has more elements than it actually does
Using len(list) as an index instead of len(list) - 1
debugging_steps: Print len(list) right before the failing line
Print the index value being used
Check loop bounds — range(len(list)) is valid, range(len(list)+1) is not
Confirm the list actually contains the expected number of items at this point in the program
fix_pattern: Adjust the index or loop range so it never exceeds len(list) - 1, or add a bounds check before accessing the element.
learning_concept: List indexing and zero-based indexing in Python
practice_seed: Give the user a loop that goes one index too far, and ask them to fix the off-by-one error.

common_triggers: KeyError exception raised when accessing a dictionary
dictionary key not found in dict lookup
missing key when indexing a dict with square brackets
explanation: Python raised a KeyError, a dictionary-specific exception, because the code tried to access a dictionary key that doesn't exist.
likely_causes: The key was misspelled or has different casing than expected
The key was never added to the dictionary
The dictionary structure changed (e.g. from an API response) and the key is no longer present
The code assumes a key exists without checking first
debugging_steps: Print the dictionary right before the failing line to see its actual keys
Compare the expected key spelling/case to the actual keys present
Check if the key is conditionally added elsewhere in the code
Use .get() to inspect whether the key is truly missing versus None
fix_pattern: Use dict.get(key, default) for optional keys, or verify the key exists with 'if key in dict' before accessing it directly.
learning_concept: Python dictionaries and safe key access
practice_seed: Give the user a snippet that accesses a dict key that may not exist, and ask them to make it safe using .get().

explanation: Python raised this because the code tried to use a method or attribute that doesn't exist on that object's type.
likely_causes: The object is actually None, often because an earlier function returned nothing
A typo in the method or attribute name
The object is a different type than the developer assumed
Using a method that exists on a similar but different type (e.g. list method on a string)
debugging_steps: Print type(object) right before the failing line
Check whether the object could be None due to an earlier function call
Check the spelling of the attribute or method name against the documentation
Trace back to where the object was created or last modified
fix_pattern: Confirm the object's type and that it isn't None before calling the attribute or method; correct typos; use the right type's API.
learning_concept: Python object types and None handling
practice_seed: Give the user a function that sometimes returns None, causing a later .append() call to fail, and ask them to fix it.

explanation: Python raised this because it could not find a module or package being imported.
likely_causes: The package isn't installed in the current environment
The package is installed in a different Python environment/virtualenv than the one running
A typo in the import statement or module name
The module is a local file that isn't in the expected directory or on the path
debugging_steps: Check the exact spelling of the module name in the error
Confirm the package is installed (pip show <package>) in the active environment
Check which Python/virtualenv is currently active
If it's a local file, confirm it's in the same directory or properly added to sys.path
fix_pattern: Install the missing package in the active environment, correct the import name, or fix the file/module path.
learning_concept: Python environments, virtual environments, and package installation
practice_seed: Give the user an import statement for an uninstalled package and ask them to describe the correct pip install command.

common_triggers: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces
explanation: Python raised this because the code's indentation doesn't follow a consistent, valid structure — Python uses indentation to define code blocks.
likely_causes: Mixing tabs and spaces in the same file
A block (if/for/def/etc.) that isn't followed by an indented line
Copy-pasted code bringing in different indentation levels
An extra or missing indent on a single line
debugging_steps: Check the exact line number mentioned in the error
Look for mixed tabs/spaces (many editors can show whitespace characters)
Confirm every colon-ending line (if, for, def, etc.) is followed by an indented block
Reformat the file consistently using 4 spaces per indent level (PEP 8)
fix_pattern: Make indentation consistent (spaces only, per PEP 8) and ensure every block header has an indented body.
learning_concept: Python's block structure and PEP 8 indentation conventions
practice_seed: Give the user a snippet with mixed tabs/spaces and ask them to fix the indentation.

common_triggers: could not convert string to float
explanation: Python raised this because a function received an argument of the right type but an inappropriate or unconvertible value.
likely_causes: Trying to convert a non-numeric string to int/float
Passing an unexpected value to a function with restricted valid inputs
User input that wasn't validated before conversion
Data from a file or API that doesn't match the expected format
debugging_steps: Print the exact value being passed right before the failing line
Check whether the value's source (user input, file, API) is validated
Check the function's documentation for what values it accepts
Add a try/except around the conversion to handle bad input gracefully
fix_pattern: Validate or sanitize the value before conversion, and handle invalid cases explicitly rather than assuming well-formed input.
learning_concept: Input validation and safe type conversion in Python
practice_seed: Give the user a snippet that crashes on int(input()) with non-numeric input, and ask them to add validation.

explanation: Python raised this because the code attempted to divide a number by zero, which is mathematically undefined.
likely_causes: A divisor variable was computed as zero unexpectedly (e.g. an empty list's length)
User input included zero without validation
A calculation assumes a non-zero denominator that isn't guaranteed
debugging_steps: Print the divisor value right before the failing line
Trace back to where the divisor is computed or supplied
Check whether the divisor can legitimately be zero in valid program states
Add a guard clause to handle the zero case explicitly
fix_pattern: Add a conditional check for zero before dividing, and decide on sensible fallback behavior (e.g. return 0, raise a clearer error, or skip the calculation).
learning_concept: Guarding against edge cases in arithmetic operations
practice_seed: Give the user a function computing an average that fails on an empty list, and ask them to guard against division by zero.

explanation: Python raised this because it tried to open a file at a path that doesn't exist from where the program is running.
likely_causes: A relative path is used, but the working directory isn't what the developer assumed
A typo in the filename or path
The file was never created or was deleted/moved
Case-sensitivity mismatch (common when moving between Windows and Linux/Mac)
debugging_steps: Print the exact path being used and compare it to the file's actual location
Check the current working directory (os.getcwd())
Confirm the file exists at that path using a file explorer or os.path.exists()
Prefer absolute paths or paths built with os.path/pathlib during debugging
fix_pattern: Correct the path (ideally using pathlib for cross-platform safety), or confirm the file exists before attempting to open it.
learning_concept: File paths, working directories, and the pathlib module
practice_seed: Give the user a snippet that opens a file using a relative path that breaks when run from a different directory, and ask them to fix it.

explanation: Python raised this because the code doesn't follow the language's grammar rules — the parser couldn't understand it before even running it.
likely_causes: A missing colon after if/for/while/def/class
Mismatched or missing parentheses, brackets, or quotes
A missing comma between items in a list, tuple, or function call
Using a Python keyword (e.g. 'class', 'print' in Py2 style) incorrectly
debugging_steps: Look at the line number in the error, then check the line just above it too — the real problem often starts earlier
Count opening and closing parentheses/brackets/quotes on the line
Check that every block-starting statement ends with a colon
Check for missing commas between function arguments or list/tuple items
fix_pattern: Correct the malformed syntax — add the missing colon, comma, or matching bracket/quote — then re-run to confirm the file parses.
learning_concept: Python syntax rules and how the parser reads code before execution
practice_seed: Give the user an if-statement missing its trailing colon and ask them to fix it.

explanation: Python raised this because a function kept calling itself without ever reaching a condition that stops the recursion, exceeding the interpreter's call-stack limit.
likely_causes: The recursive function is missing a base case (a stopping condition)
The base case exists but is never actually reached due to a logic error
Each recursive call doesn't move the input closer to the base case
The problem doesn't actually need recursion and an iterative loop would be simpler and safer
debugging_steps: Identify the function's base case — the condition where it should stop calling itself
Add a print statement showing the argument value on each call to see if it's converging toward the base case
Check that every recursive call passes a genuinely smaller/simpler input
Consider whether a loop would solve the problem more safely than recursion
fix_pattern: Add or fix the base case so recursion terminates, and ensure each recursive call moves measurably closer to it.
learning_concept: Recursion, base cases, and the call stack
practice_seed: Give the user a factorial function missing its base case and ask them to add it so recursion terminates.
